analysis.one_liner: Bans the gasoline additive MTBE and funds cleanup of contaminated drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban the gasoline additive MTBE was referred to a House subcommittee in March 2000, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the EPA to ban MTBE, a gasoline additive that leaks from underground tanks and contaminates groundwater, by January 1, 2004. It required tank owners to monitor for MTBE after any leak, sped up tank enforcement in contaminated areas, and let the EPA declare drinking-water emergencies in MTBE-affected communities and issue federal grants for clean water and cleanup. It also directed a federal health study of long-term MTBE exposure.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from wells and public water supplies near leaking gas station and storage tanks, especially in states like New York and California where MTBE has fouled groundwater. Local governments would get federal grants to connect contaminated wells to clean public water, buy bottled water, and remediate supplies.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to prohibit MTBE as a fuel additive by no later than January 1, 2004, and to bar any newly registered gasoline additive unless scientific testing and peer review show no adverse public effects.

Requires underground tank owners to monitor for MTBE after any leak is detected and report results annually for at least ten years, and directs EPA enforcement focus to areas where MTBE is leaking into groundwater or surface water.

Lets the EPA declare a drinking-water emergency on a Governor's or local official's request and issue expedited grants to connect people with contaminated wells to public water, buy bottled water, and remediate community water supplies.
Directs the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to study the long-term health effects of MTBE in drinking water.

analysis.who_pays: Gasoline refiners and MTBE producers, who would lose the additive market and face tighter cleanup enforcement, with costs likely passed partly into fuel prices. Tank owners would bear new monitoring costs. The bill pays for its water grants by cutting $15 million from the Army School of the Americas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Refiners, MTBE makers, and tank owners

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves the Clean Air Act's oxygenate requirement, so refiners would have to substitute another additive (in practice, mainly ethanol), which critics warned could raise fuel costs in some regions.
Mandated MTBE monitoring and accelerated tank cleanup would impose real compliance costs on tank owners, including small gas stations, that could be passed to consumers.
The bill funds its $15 million water-grant program by reducing FY 2001 money for the Army School of the Americas, a tradeoff unrelated to water safety that some legislators opposed on its own terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial: MTBE moves quickly through groundwater, and contaminated wells force households onto bottled water or expensive hookups, so a federal ban plus cleanup grants addresses a real public-health problem. The costs fall mainly on the refining and storage-tank industries, though some could reach pump prices. The design is imperfect — it keeps the oxygenate mandate rather than repealing it, and it attaches a controversial defense-school cut as a budget offset — but the trade is broadly favorable to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Forbes introduced the bill on March 1, 2000, joined by eleven cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican).
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day, and on March 13, 2000 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action — no markup, hearing vote, or floor vote — appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

Separate from Congress, the fight over MTBE continued for years: the additive was eventually phased out state by state, and EPA later declined a 2000s-era petition to ban it outright, leaving cleanup largely to states and courts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: MTBE producers and refiners kept using the additive with no federal phase-out deadline, and tank owners avoided new monitoring duties. Communities with contaminated water got no federal emergency grants, and the health study was never ordered through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Michael P. Forbes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed to ban MTBE and fund contaminated-water cleanup.

against.name: House Commerce Committee / Health and Environment Subcommittee
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled whether the bill got a hearing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 1, 2000 and referred it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it died without a markup or vote.

against.name: Petroleum refining and MTBE manufacturers
against.role: Industry with the additive market and cleanup liability at stake
against.what_they_did: Faced losing the MTBE market under a 2004 ban and new monitoring and enforcement duties; industry opposition to federal MTBE bans was widely reported during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and 10 of the 11 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Republican, leaving the true partisan shape untested.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the MTBE additive market by 2004 and tightened leak enforcement on tank owners. The industry's interest in keeping the additive on the market ran directly against communities whose water it contaminated.

industries.industry: Underground storage tank owners and operators (gas stations, fuel distributors)
industries.note: New mandatory MTBE monitoring after any leak, plus focused EPA enforcement of tank upgrades, would raise compliance costs — costs these businesses could pass to customers at the pump.

industries.industry: Environmental remediation and water treatment firms
industries.note: Emergency grants for cleanup, well connections, and water remediation would create demand for cleanup work; their gain tracks the public's interest in clean water.
Utilities would receive federal grants to remediate supplies and absorb well users, but would also face accelerated testing and reporting duties for MTBE.
